# How to use this guide

Study one unit a day: read the notes, practise drawing every diagram once from memory, then answer the question bank without looking. Each unit has Short Answer (5-mark) and Long Essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in pharmacy university papers.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ or very short answers | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with diagrams.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

**Scoring tips**

1. Draw the structure or mechanism first, then explain. Examiners give marks for every correct step and arrow.
2. In a mechanism, always show: electrophile generation → attack on ring → carbocation (sigma complex) → loss of H+.
3. Write reagents and conditions on the arrow (e.g. conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4, 50 °C).
4. End every essay with 3–4 uses or examples; pharmacy examiners look for the drug link.
5. Underline key words: *resonance*, *electrophile*, *ortho/para director*, *sigma complex*.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics with full diagrams: **substituent effects in EAS**, **diazonium salt applications**, **iodine + saponification + acid value**, **Haworth synthesis of naphthalene**, and **Baeyer strain theory with limitations**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Named reactions and their one-line meaning**

| Name | Reagents | Result | Unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Friedel–Crafts alkylation | R–Cl + AlCl3 | Alkylbenzene (rearranges, polyalkylates) | 1 |
| Friedel–Crafts acylation | RCOCl + AlCl3 | Aryl ketone (no rearrangement) | 1 |
| Clemmensen reduction | Zn-Hg / HCl | C=O → CH2 | 1, 4 |
| Remsen–Fahlberg | Toluene → ClSO3H → NH3 → KMnO4 → heat | Saccharin | 1 |
| Kolbe–Schmidt | Sodium phenoxide + CO2 | Salicylic acid | 2 |
| Reimer–Tiemann | Phenol + CHCl3 + NaOH | Salicylaldehyde | 2 |
| Liebermann nitroso test | Phenol + NaNO2 + H2SO4 | Green → red → blue | 2 |
| Diazotisation | ArNH2 + NaNO2 + HCl, 0–5 °C | ArN2+ Cl− | 2 |
| Sandmeyer | ArN2+ + CuCl / CuBr / CuCN | ArCl / ArBr / ArCN | 2 |
| Gattermann | ArN2+ + Cu powder + HX | ArX | 2 |
| Balz–Schiemann | ArN2+ + HBF4, heat | ArF | 2 |
| Wijs method | ICl in acetic acid | Iodine value | 3 |
| Haworth (naphthalene) | Benzene + succinic anhydride | Naphthalene | 4 |
| Haworth (phenanthrene) | Naphthalene + succinic anhydride | Phenanthrene | 4 |
| Pschorr | Diazotised o-amino-α-phenylcinnamic acid + Cu | Phenanthrene | 4 |
| Elbs | Pyrolysis of o-methyl diaryl ketone | Anthracene | 4 |
| Gomberg | Trityl chloride + Ag/Zn | Triphenylmethyl radical | 4 |
| Freund | 1,3-Dibromopropane + Zn | Cyclopropane | 5 |
| Simmons–Smith | Alkene + CH2I2 + Zn-Cu | Cyclopropane | 5 |

**Numbers worth memorising**

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Benzene C–C bond length | 1.39 Å (single 1.54, double 1.34) |
| Benzene resonance energy | 36 kcal/mol (150 kJ/mol) |
| pKa: phenol / benzoic acid / acetic acid / picric acid | 10 / 4.2 / 4.76 / 0.4 |
| pKb: aniline / ammonia / methylamine | 9.4 / 4.75 / 3.4 |
| Resonance energy: naphthalene / anthracene / phenanthrene | 61 / 84 / 92 kcal/mol |
| Angle deviation: cyclopropane / cyclobutane / cyclopentane | 24°44' / 9°44' / 0°44' |
| Chair → boat energy gap | 6.9 kcal/mol |
| Iodine value classes | < 100 non-drying, 100–130 semi-drying, > 130 drying |
| RM value of butter | 17–35 (other fats < 1) |
| Saccharin sweetness | 300–500 × sugar |

**Common traps in MCQs**

- Halogens: **deactivating but ortho/para directing**.
- Benzene + Cl2: **FeCl3 → substitution** (chlorobenzene); **sunlight → addition** (BHC).
- BHC is a **cyclohexane**, not a benzene; only the **γ-isomer (lindane)** is active.
- Phenol does **not** react with NaHCO3; benzoic acid does.
- **Ortho effect**: ortho-substituted benzoic acids are stronger; ortho-substituted anilines are weaker.
- Naphthalene sulfonation: **80 °C → 1-**, **160 °C → 2-sulfonic acid**.
- Anthracene and phenanthrene react at **C9 and C10**.
- Baeyer predicted cyclopentane most stable; really **cyclohexane** is.
- Cyclopropane decolourises Br2 but **not** cold KMnO4.
- Acid value = **free** acid; saponification value = **free + combined** acid; ester value = SV − AV.

| Azo coupling | Prontosil, methyl orange |
| Chloramine-T | Antiseptic, water disinfection |
| Lindane | Scabies and lice lotion |
| Naphthalene ring | Naproxen, propranolol, menadione (vit K3) |
| Anthraquinone | Senna laxatives, doxorubicin |
| Phenanthrene (reduced) | Steroids, morphine |
| Benzhydryl / trityl | Diphenhydramine, cetirizine / clotrimazole, gentian violet |
| Antioxidants vs rancidity | BHA, BHT, vitamin E in oily injections |
| Cyclopropyl ring | Ciprofloxacin |

# Recrystallisation and melting point

**Aim:** To purify crude benzoic acid by recrystallisation from water and find its melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

A solid is far more soluble in a hot solvent than in the same solvent cold. Dissolve the crude solid in the least hot solvent, filter off insoluble dirt while hot, and let it cool. The pure compound crystallises; soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor. A pure solid melts sharply (within 1–2 °C); impurities lower the melting point and widen the range.

## Requirements

Crude benzoic acid (2 g), distilled water, activated charcoal, beakers, funnel, fluted filter paper, Büchner funnel and suction, capillary tubes, Thiele tube with liquid paraffin, thermometer.

## Procedure

1. Put 2 g crude benzoic acid in a beaker with about 40 ml water. Heat to boiling and stir; add hot water in small portions until it just dissolves.
2. If coloured, cool slightly, add a pinch of charcoal and boil 2–3 minutes.
3. Filter hot through a fluted paper in a warmed funnel.
4. Let the filtrate cool slowly to room temperature, then in ice.
5. Collect the crystals by suction, wash with a little ice-cold water, and dry.
6. Fill a capillary sealed at one end to about 3 mm with the dry powder. Tie it to the thermometer, heat the Thiele tube slowly (about 2 °C a minute near the melting point), and note the temperatures at which melting starts and ends.

## Result

Weight of pure benzoic acid: ___ g. Practical yield = (weight obtained ÷ weight taken) × 100 = ___ %.
Melting point: ___ °C (reported: 122 °C).

## Precautions

- Use the minimum hot solvent, or much product stays dissolved.
- Never add charcoal to a boiling solution; it froths over.
- Cool slowly for bigger, purer crystals.
- Heat slowly near the melting point.

## Viva questions

1. **What makes a good recrystallisation solvent?** Dissolves the compound well hot and poorly cold, does not react with it, dissolves impurities or not at all, and is easy to remove.
2. **Why use a fluted filter paper and a warm funnel?** Fast filtration, so crystals do not form in the funnel.
3. **What does charcoal do?** Adsorbs coloured impurities.
4. **What does a low, wide melting range show?** The sample is impure or wet.
5. **What is mixed melting point?** Mixing the sample with an authentic sample: no fall in melting point means they are the same compound.

# Steam distillation

**Aim:** To purify a steam-volatile organic liquid (for example nitrobenzene or aniline) by steam distillation.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves. Nitrobenzene and aniline are toxic through the skin; handle them in a fume hood.

## Principle

When two immiscible liquids are heated together, each exerts its own vapour pressure. The mixture boils when the sum equals atmospheric pressure, so it boils **below 100 °C** and below the boiling point of the organic liquid. A high-boiling, water-insoluble compound therefore distils with steam at under 100 °C without decomposing. Non-volatile impurities stay behind.

Weight ratio in the distillate: w(organic) ÷ w(water) = (p(organic) × M(organic)) ÷ (p(water) × 18).

## Requirements

Steam generator (or boiling flask with water), round-bottom flask with the impure liquid, long condenser, receiver, separating funnel, anhydrous CaCl2, safety tube.

## Procedure

1. Put the impure liquid with a little water in the round-bottom flask, tilted, and connect it to the steam generator and condenser.
2. Pass steam. Heat the flask gently so water does not collect.
3. Collect the milky distillate until it runs clear.
4. Separate the organic layer in a separating funnel, dry it over anhydrous CaCl2 and weigh it.

## Result

Volume or weight of purified liquid: ___.

## Precautions

- Keep a safety tube in the steam generator.
- Stop by disconnecting the steam line before turning off heat, or liquid sucks back.
- Use a long, efficient condenser.

## Viva questions

1. **Which compounds suit steam distillation?** Water-insoluble, steam-volatile, with a reasonable vapour pressure near 100 °C, and stable to steam.
2. **Why does the mixture boil below 100 °C?** The vapour pressures add up, so atmospheric pressure is reached at a lower temperature.
3. **Give pharmaceutical uses.** Volatile oils (clove, eucalyptus), purifying aniline and nitrobenzene, separating o-nitrophenol from p-nitrophenol.
4. **Why is o-nitrophenol steam-volatile but p-nitrophenol not?** The ortho isomer has intramolecular hydrogen bonding; the para isomer is held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

# Acid value of an oil

**Aim:** To determine the acid value of the given oil (for example castor oil).

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Acid value is the number of milligrams of KOH needed to neutralise the **free** fatty acids in 1 g of oil. The oil is dissolved in neutral alcohol–ether and titrated with standard alkali using phenolphthalein. A high acid value shows hydrolytic rancidity or poor refining.

RCOOH + KOH → RCOOK + H2O

## Requirements

Oil, ethanol–ether (1:1) neutralised to phenolphthalein, 0.1 N KOH (or NaOH), phenolphthalein, conical flask, burette, balance.

## Procedure

1. Weigh about 5 g oil (W) into a conical flask.
2. Add 50 ml of the neutralised ethanol–ether and shake until the oil dissolves (warm gently if needed).
3. Add a few drops of phenolphthalein and titrate with 0.1 N KOH, shaking, until a faint pink lasts 30 seconds.
4. Note the volume (V ml). Repeat for concordant readings.

## Calculation

Acid value = (56.1 × N × V) ÷ W

where N is the normality of KOH and 56.1 the molecular weight of KOH.

## Result

The acid value of the given oil is ___ mg KOH/g.

## Viva questions

1. **Define acid value.** Mg of KOH to neutralise the free fatty acids in 1 g of fat or oil.
2. **Why neutralise the solvent first?** So only the acids from the oil use up the alkali.
3. **Why does acid value rise on storage?** Lipase or moisture hydrolyses the glycerides into free fatty acids (hydrolytic rancidity).
4. **How is acid value related to free fatty acid %?** FFA % (as oleic acid) is about acid value ÷ 2.

# Saponification value of an oil

**Aim:** To determine the saponification value of the given oil.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Saponification value is the number of milligrams of KOH needed to saponify 1 g of oil, that is, to neutralise both free and combined (ester) fatty acids. The oil is refluxed with a known excess of alcoholic KOH, and the KOH left over is titrated with standard HCl. A blank without oil gives the total KOH taken.

Triglyceride + 3 KOH → glycerol + 3 RCOOK (soap)

A high value means short-chain fatty acids (low molecular weight), as in coconut oil.

## Requirements

Oil, 0.5 N alcoholic KOH, 0.5 N HCl, phenolphthalein, two round-bottom flasks with reflux condensers, water bath, burette, pipette.

## Procedure

1. Weigh about 2 g oil (W) into a round-bottom flask.
2. Pipette 25 ml of 0.5 N alcoholic KOH into it, and 25 ml into a second flask with no oil (blank).
3. Reflux both on a water bath for 30–60 minutes, until the oil drops disappear.
4. Cool, add phenolphthalein and titrate each with 0.5 N HCl until the pink just disappears.
5. Note the readings: blank B ml, sample S ml.

## Calculation

Saponification value = (56.1 × N × (B − S)) ÷ W

where N is the normality of HCl.

## Result

The saponification value of the given oil is ___ mg KOH/g.

## Viva questions

1. **Why run a blank?** Alcoholic KOH changes strength on standing; the blank gives the exact KOH taken.
2. **What does saponification value tell you?** The average chain length (molecular weight) of the fatty acids.
3. **What is ester value?** Saponification value minus acid value.
4. **Why alcoholic and not aqueous KOH?** Oil dissolves in alcohol, so the reaction is faster and complete.

# Iodine value of an oil (Wijs method)

**Aim:** To determine the iodine value of the given oil by the Wijs method.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves. Keep Wijs solution and chloroform in the fume hood.

## Principle

Iodine value is the number of grams of iodine absorbed by 100 g of oil. It measures unsaturation. Iodine monochloride (Wijs solution) adds across the C=C bonds. The unused ICl is turned into iodine by KI, and the iodine is titrated with standard sodium thiosulfate using starch. A blank gives the total ICl taken.

ICl + KI → KCl + I2;  I2 + 2 Na2S2O3 → 2 NaI + Na2S4O6

## Requirements

Oil, chloroform (or carbon tetrachloride / cyclohexane as your lab uses), Wijs solution, 10% KI, 0.1 N sodium thiosulfate, starch indicator, iodine flasks with stoppers, pipettes, burette.

## Procedure

1. Weigh 0.1–0.5 g oil (W) into an iodine flask; take less for highly unsaturated oils. Dissolve in 10 ml chloroform.
2. Pipette 25 ml Wijs solution in, stopper, swirl, and keep in the dark for 30 minutes. Set up a blank the same way without oil.
3. Add 15 ml 10% KI and 100 ml water to each.
4. Titrate with 0.1 N thiosulfate until pale yellow, add starch, and continue until the blue just disappears.
5. Note the readings: blank B ml, sample S ml.

## Calculation

Iodine value = (12.69 × N × (B − S)) ÷ W

where N is the normality of thiosulfate (12.69 = 126.9 × 100 ÷ 1000).

## Result

The iodine value of the given oil is ___ g iodine/100 g. Class: non-drying (< 100), semi-drying (100–130) or drying (> 130).

## Viva questions

1. **Why keep the flasks in the dark?** Light causes side reactions and loss of iodine.
2. **Why add starch only near the end?** At high iodine concentration the starch–iodine complex forms and does not release iodine easily, giving a late end point.
3. **Why use ICl rather than iodine alone?** Iodine adds slowly and incompletely; ICl is more reactive.
4. **Name a drying oil and a non-drying oil.** Linseed oil (drying), olive or castor oil (non-drying).

# Benzanilide from aniline (benzoylation)

**Aim:** To prepare benzanilide from aniline by the Schotten–Baumann reaction.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves. Benzoyl chloride is a lachrymator and aniline is toxic; work in the fume hood.

## Principle

An amine reacts with an acid chloride in aqueous alkali (Schotten–Baumann). The alkali neutralises the HCl formed and destroys excess benzoyl chloride.

C6H5NH2 + C6H5COCl + NaOH → C6H5NHCOC6H5 + NaCl + H2O

## Requirements

Aniline 2 ml, benzoyl chloride 3 ml, 10% NaOH 25 ml, stoppered conical flask, Büchner funnel, ethanol for recrystallisation.

## Procedure

1. Put 2 ml aniline and 25 ml 10% NaOH in a stoppered conical flask.
2. Add 3 ml benzoyl chloride in small portions, stoppering and shaking hard after each addition.
3. Keep shaking for about 15 minutes, until the smell of benzoyl chloride is gone. The solution must stay alkaline.
4. Filter the solid, wash well with cold water, and dry.
5. Recrystallise from hot ethanol.

## Result

Theoretical yield (from 2 ml aniline, about 2.04 g, M 93): (2.04 ÷ 93) × 197 ≈ 4.3 g.
Practical yield: ___ g (___ %). Melting point: ___ °C (reported: 163 °C).

## Viva questions

1. **What is the Schotten–Baumann reaction?** Acylation of amines, alcohols or phenols with an acid chloride in aqueous alkali.
2. **Why NaOH?** It neutralises HCl and keeps the amine free to react; it also hydrolyses leftover benzoyl chloride.
3. **Why add benzoyl chloride slowly?** The reaction is exothermic.
4. **Pharmaceutical use of acylation?** Protecting –NH2 groups during synthesis, e.g. acetanilide in sulfonamide synthesis.
practicals.title: Benzanilide from aniline (benzoylation)

# p-Bromoacetanilide from acetanilide (bromination)

**Aim:** To prepare p-bromoacetanilide from acetanilide.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves. Bromine is corrosive and toxic; use it only in the fume hood. Many labs make bromine in situ from KBr and KBrO3 instead.

## Principle

–NHCOCH3 is a moderately activating ortho/para director. Its bulk hinders the ortho position, so bromine enters mainly at para. Unlike the free –NH2 group of aniline, it does not give a tribromo product.

C6H5NHCOCH3 + Br2 → p-BrC6H4NHCOCH3 + HBr

## Requirements

Acetanilide 2 g, glacial acetic acid 10 ml, bromine in glacial acetic acid (about 1 ml Br2 in 5 ml), ice water, Büchner funnel, ethanol.

## Procedure

1. Dissolve 2 g acetanilide in 10 ml glacial acetic acid in a conical flask.
2. Add the bromine solution drop by drop with shaking until a faint yellow colour stays.
3. Leave 15 minutes, then pour into about 100 ml ice-cold water with stirring.
4. Filter, wash with cold water (add a little sodium bisulfite if it is still yellow), and dry.
5. Recrystallise from ethanol.

## Result

Theoretical yield: (2 ÷ 135) × 214 ≈ 3.2 g. Practical yield: ___ g (___ %). Melting point: ___ °C (reported: 167 °C).

## Viva questions

1. **Why acetanilide and not aniline?** Aniline is so activating that it gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline; the acetyl group tames it and the product is mono-brominated.
2. **Why is the para product major?** The bulky –NHCOCH3 group blocks the ortho positions.
3. **Why glacial acetic acid?** It dissolves both reactants and is not attacked by bromine.
4. **How do you get p-bromoaniline from the product?** Hydrolyse the amide with acid or alkali.
practicals.title: p-Bromoacetanilide from acetanilide (bromination)

# 1-Phenylazo-2-naphthol (diazotisation and coupling)

**Aim:** To prepare 1-phenylazo-2-naphthol, an orange-red azo dye, from aniline.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves. Keep the diazonium solution cold and use it at once; never let it dry.

## Principle

Aniline is diazotised with nitrous acid (NaNO2 + HCl) at 0–5 °C to benzenediazonium chloride. This weak electrophile couples with 2-naphthol in alkaline solution at C1, giving the azo dye.

C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2 HCl → C6H5N2+Cl− + NaCl + 2 H2O
C6H5N2+Cl− + 2-naphthol (NaOH) → 1-phenylazo-2-naphthol + NaCl + H2O

## Requirements

Aniline 2 ml, conc. HCl 5 ml, sodium nitrite 1.6 g, 2-naphthol 3 g, 10% NaOH 25 ml, ice, starch–iodide paper, beakers, Büchner funnel.

## Procedure

1. Mix 2 ml aniline with 5 ml conc. HCl and 5 ml water; cool to 0–5 °C in ice.
2. Dissolve 1.6 g NaNO2 in 8 ml water and add it drop by drop, keeping below 5 °C, until starch–iodide paper turns blue (slight excess of nitrous acid).
3. Dissolve 3 g 2-naphthol in 25 ml 10% NaOH and cool in ice.
4. Pour the diazonium solution slowly into the naphthol solution with stirring. An orange-red solid forms.
5. Stir 15 minutes in ice, filter, wash with cold water, and dry. Recrystallise from ethanol if asked.

## Result

Practical yield: ___ g. Colour: orange-red. Melting point: ___ °C (reported: about 131 °C).

## Viva questions

1. **Why 0–5 °C?** Above this the diazonium salt loses N2 and forms phenol.
2. **What is the starch–iodide test for?** Free nitrous acid oxidises iodide to iodine, showing diazotisation is complete.
3. **Why couple in alkali?** 2-Naphthol becomes the naphthoxide ion, which is much more reactive.
4. **Where does coupling happen on 2-naphthol?** At C1 (the α-position next to –OH).
5. **Pharmaceutical relevance?** Prontosil (first sulfa drug) is an azo dye; the Bratton–Marshall assay of sulfonamides uses diazotisation and coupling.
practicals.title: 1-Phenylazo-2-naphthol (diazotisation and coupling)

# Salicylic acid from methyl salicylate (hydrolysis)

**Aim:** To prepare salicylic acid by alkaline hydrolysis of methyl salicylate.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Esters are hydrolysed by hot alkali to the alcohol and the salt of the acid (saponification). Acidifying the salt precipitates the free acid.

C6H4(OH)COOCH3 + 2 NaOH → C6H4(ONa)COONa + CH3OH + H2O
C6H4(ONa)COONa + 2 HCl → C6H4(OH)COOH + 2 NaCl

## Requirements

Methyl salicylate 2 ml, 10% NaOH 25 ml, conc. HCl, round-bottom flask with reflux condenser, ice, Büchner funnel.

## Procedure

1. Reflux 2 ml methyl salicylate with 25 ml 10% NaOH for about 30 minutes, until the oily drops disappear.
2. Cool, then add conc. HCl slowly with stirring until the solution is acidic to litmus. White salicylic acid separates.
3. Cool in ice, filter, wash with a little cold water, and dry.
4. Recrystallise from hot water.

## Result

Theoretical yield (2 ml methyl salicylate ≈ 2.36 g, M 152): (2.36 ÷ 152) × 138 ≈ 2.1 g.
Practical yield: ___ g (___ %). Melting point: ___ °C (reported: about 158 °C).

## Viva questions

1. **Why does methyl salicylate need two moles of NaOH?** One for the ester group, one for the acidic phenolic –OH.
2. **How do you know hydrolysis is complete?** The oily layer and its wintergreen smell disappear.
3. **Test for salicylic acid?** Violet colour with neutral FeCl3 (phenolic –OH).
4. **Uses?** Keratolytic (corn and wart removers), and the starting material for aspirin.
practicals.title: Salicylic acid from methyl salicylate (hydrolysis)

# Dibenzalacetone (Claisen–Schmidt condensation)

**Aim:** To prepare dibenzalacetone from benzaldehyde and acetone.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

In alkali, acetone forms an enolate that adds to benzaldehyde (which has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot condense with itself). Dehydration gives benzalacetone, and repeating on the other side of acetone gives dibenzalacetone (1,5-diphenylpenta-1,4-dien-3-one).

2 C6H5CHO + CH3COCH3 → C6H5CH=CHCOCH=CHC6H5 + 2 H2O

## Requirements

Benzaldehyde 2.5 ml, acetone 0.9 ml, ethanol 20 ml, 10% NaOH 25 ml, conical flask, Büchner funnel.

## Procedure

1. Mix 2.5 ml benzaldehyde, 0.9 ml acetone and 20 ml ethanol in a conical flask.
2. Add 25 ml 10% NaOH and shake or stir for 15–30 minutes. A yellow solid separates.
3. Cool in ice, filter, and wash well with cold water until the washings are neutral.
4. Dry, then recrystallise from ethanol.

## Result

Practical yield: ___ g. Colour: pale yellow. Melting point: ___ °C (reported: about 111 °C).

## Viva questions

1. **Why does benzaldehyde not self-condense?** It has no α-hydrogen to form an enolate.
2. **Why 2 moles of benzaldehyde per mole of acetone?** Acetone has α-hydrogens on both sides, so it condenses twice.
3. **What is the base for?** It removes an α-hydrogen from acetone to form the enolate.
4. **Name another condensation of benzaldehyde.** Perkin reaction (with acetic anhydride and sodium acetate) gives cinnamic acid.
practicals.title: Dibenzalacetone (Claisen–Schmidt condensation)

# Unit 1: Benzene and its derivatives

Benzene (C6H6) is a flat ring of six carbons whose six π electrons are shared by the whole ring. That sharing makes it unusually stable, so it prefers **substitution** (keep the ring) over **addition** (break the ring).

## 1.1 Structure of benzene

**Kekulé structure (1865).** A six-membered ring with alternating single and double bonds. Kekulé said the double bonds keep switching between two positions.

**Why Kekulé alone fails:**

- Benzene does not decolourise bromine water or cold KMnO4, unlike real alkenes.
- Only **one** ortho-disubstituted product exists (one 1,2-dibromobenzene). Fixed double bonds would give two.
- All six C–C bonds are the **same length, 1.39 Å**. That sits between a C–C single (1.54 Å) and a C=C double bond (1.34 Å).
- Benzene is about **36 kcal/mol (150 kJ/mol)** more stable than expected (resonance energy).

**Resonance energy from heats of hydrogenation**

| Compound | Heat of hydrogenation |
| --- | --- |
| Cyclohexene (1 C=C) | 28.6 kcal/mol |
| "Cyclohexatriene" expected (3 × 28.6) | 85.8 kcal/mol |
| Benzene actually measured | 49.8 kcal/mol |
| Difference = resonance energy | 36 kcal/mol |

**Resonance (modern) picture.** Benzene is a **resonance hybrid** of the two Kekulé structures. The real molecule is neither; it is an average, drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside.

```text
Draw in the exam:

   Kekulé I   <-->   Kekulé II     =     Hybrid
    ___               ___                 ___
   //  \             /  \\               / o \     (circle = 6 shared π electrons)
  ||    ||          |    |               |     |
   \\__//            \\__//              \___/
```

**Orbital picture (draw this for 5 marks).**

1. Each carbon is **sp2 hybridised**: bond angle 120°, so the ring is a flat regular hexagon.
2. sp2 orbitals form six C–C σ bonds and six C–H σ bonds.
3. Each carbon keeps one unhybridised **p orbital** standing perpendicular to the ring.
4. The six p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring.
5. Result: two doughnut-shaped **π electron clouds**, one above and one below the plane, holding six delocalised electrons.

```text
        ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~      <- π cloud above the ring
     C---C---C---C---C---C  (flat hexagon of σ bonds, side view)
        ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~      <- π cloud below the ring
```

*Real-life link:* this cloud of shared electrons is why benzene rings appear in so many drugs (paracetamol, aspirin, diazepam): the ring is stable in the body and gives a flat surface that fits receptor pockets.

## 1.2 Aromaticity and Hückel's rule

A compound is **aromatic** when it meets all four conditions:

1. **Cyclic** — atoms joined in a ring.
2. **Planar** — the ring is flat.
3. **Fully conjugated** — every ring atom has a p orbital in the π system.
4. **Hückel's rule** — it has **(4n + 2) π electrons**, where n = 0, 1, 2, 3 … (2, 6, 10, 14 … electrons).

If conditions 1–3 hold but there are **4n π electrons** (4, 8 …), the compound is **antiaromatic** (very unstable). If the ring is not flat or not fully conjugated, it is **non-aromatic**.

| Compound | π electrons | n | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Benzene | 6 | 1 | Aromatic |
| Naphthalene | 10 | 2 | Aromatic |
| Anthracene, phenanthrene | 14 | 3 | Aromatic |
| Pyridine, pyrrole, furan, thiophene | 6 | 1 | Aromatic (heterocycles) |
| Cyclopentadienyl anion | 6 | 1 | Aromatic |
| Tropylium (cycloheptatrienyl) cation | 6 | 1 | Aromatic |
| Cyclopropenyl cation | 2 | 0 | Aromatic |
| Cyclobutadiene | 4 | — | Antiaromatic |
| Cyclooctatetraene | 8 | — | Non-aromatic (tub-shaped, not planar) |

**Memory trick:** "**C-P-C-H**" = Cyclic, Planar, Conjugated, Hückel.

## 1.3 Electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) — general mechanism

An **electrophile** (E+, "electron lover") replaces one H of the ring. The π cloud is rich in electrons, so it attracts electrophiles.

1. **Generate the electrophile.** A reagent plus a catalyst (acid or Lewis acid) makes E+.
2. **Attack (slow, rate-determining).** The π electrons attack E+. A positively charged, non-aromatic intermediate forms, called the **arenium ion / sigma (σ) complex / Wheland intermediate**. Its + charge is spread over three carbons by resonance (ortho and para to the new group).
3. **Lose H+ (fast).** A base removes H+ from the carbon carrying E. Aromaticity is restored.

```text
FLOWCHART — every EAS answer follows this

 Reagent + catalyst ──► E+ (electrophile)
                              │
                              ▼
 Benzene π cloud attacks E+ ──► σ-complex (arenium ion, 3 resonance forms)  [slow]
                              │
                              ▼
 Base removes H+ ──► substituted benzene (aromatic again)  [fast]
```

**Energy diagram (describe in words):** energy rises to transition state 1 → dips into the σ-complex (an intermediate valley) → rises a little to transition state 2 → falls to products. The first hump is higher, so step 2 is rate-determining.

## 1.4 The four key reactions

**(a) Nitration** — conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 ("nitrating mixture"), 50–55 °C.

```text
Electrophile:  HNO3 + 2 H2SO4  →  NO2+ (nitronium ion) + H3O+ + 2 HSO4−
Overall:       C6H6 + HNO3  —(H2SO4, 50 °C)→  C6H5NO2 (nitrobenzene) + H2O
```

H2SO4 is the stronger acid; it protonates HNO3, which then loses water to give NO2+. Keep the temperature below about 60 °C or dinitrobenzene forms. *Use:* nitrobenzene → aniline → sulpha drugs, paracetamol.

**(b) Sulfonation** — fuming H2SO4 (oleum, H2SO4 + SO3) or hot conc. H2SO4.

```text
Electrophile:  2 H2SO4  ⇌  SO3 + H3O+ + HSO4−     (SO3 is neutral but electron-poor at S)
Overall:       C6H6 + H2SO4 (SO3)  ⇌  C6H5SO3H (benzenesulfonic acid) + H2O
```

Sulfonation is **reversible**: heating with dilute acid or steam removes –SO3H (desulfonation). Chemists use this to block a position temporarily. *Use:* sulfonic acids → sulfonamide drugs, detergents.

**(c) Halogenation** — Cl2/FeCl3 (or AlCl3) or Br2/FeBr3, in the dark.

```text
Electrophile:  Cl2 + FeCl3  →  Cl+ ··· FeCl4−   (Lewis acid polarises Cl–Cl)
Overall:       C6H6 + Cl2  —(FeCl3)→  C6H5Cl (chlorobenzene) + HCl
```

Iodine is too unreactive; iodination needs an oxidising agent (HNO3) to make I+. In **sunlight without catalyst**, Cl2 **adds** instead, giving BHC (see 1.6). This contrast is a favourite MCQ.

**(d) Friedel–Crafts reactions** — Lewis acid AlCl3, anhydrous.

*Alkylation:*

```text
Electrophile:  R–Cl + AlCl3  →  R+ + AlCl4−
Example:       C6H6 + CH3Cl  —(AlCl3)→  C6H5CH3 (toluene) + HCl
```

*Acylation:*

```text
Electrophile:  R–COCl + AlCl3  →  R–C≡O+ (acylium ion, resonance-stabilised) + AlCl4−
Example:       C6H6 + CH3COCl  —(AlCl3)→  C6H5COCH3 (acetophenone) + HCl
```

**Limitations of Friedel–Crafts alkylation (very high probability):**

1. **Polyalkylation** — the alkyl group activates the ring, so the product reacts again (di-, tri-alkylbenzenes). Use excess benzene to reduce it.
2. **Carbocation rearrangement** — n-propyl chloride gives mostly **isopropylbenzene (cumene)**, because the 1° carbocation shifts to a more stable 2° one.
3. **Fails on deactivated rings** — no reaction with nitrobenzene, benzoic acid, benzaldehyde, etc. (Nitrobenzene is even used as the solvent.)
4. **Fails with –NH2, –NHR, –NR2 rings** — the lone pair on nitrogen binds AlCl3 and the ring becomes deactivated.
5. **Aryl and vinyl halides** (e.g. chlorobenzene as the halide) do not form carbocations, so they cannot alkylate.
6. **Reversible** — alkyl groups can migrate or come off.

**Why acylation is better:** the acylium ion does not rearrange, and the C=O product deactivates the ring, so no poly-acylation. To get a straight-chain alkylbenzene, acylate first, then reduce C=O to CH2 (Clemmensen: Zn-Hg/HCl, or Wolff–Kishner). Acylation needs slightly more than 1 equivalent of AlCl3 because the ketone product holds on to AlCl3.

## 1.5 Effect of substituents on reactivity and orientation

A group already on the ring decides two things: **how fast** the next substitution happens (reactivity) and **where** it goes (orientation).

**Two electronic effects:**

- **Inductive effect (I)** — pull or push of electrons through σ bonds. Electronegative atoms (–NO2, –Cl, –OH) are –I. Alkyl groups are +I.
- **Resonance / mesomeric effect (R or M)** — sharing through π orbitals. A group with a lone pair next to the ring donates (+R: –OH, –NH2, –OCH3, –Cl). A group with a π bond to an electronegative atom withdraws (–R: –NO2, –CHO, –COOH, –CN).

| Class | Groups (strongest first) | Ring becomes | Next group goes to |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strong activators | –O−, –NH2, –NHR, –NR2, –OH, –OCH3 | Much faster than benzene | Ortho + para |
| Moderate activators | –NHCOCH3, –OCOCH3 | Faster | Ortho + para |
| Weak activators | –CH3 and other alkyls, –C6H5 | Slightly faster | Ortho + para |
| Weak deactivators | –F, –Cl, –Br, –I | Slower | Ortho + para (exception) |
| Strong deactivators | –NO2, –NR3+, –CF3, –CN, –SO3H, –COOH, –COOR, –CHO, –COR | Much slower | Meta |

**Why activators send the group ortho/para (anisole example):** when E+ attacks ortho or para, one resonance form of the σ-complex puts the + charge on the carbon holding –OCH3. The oxygen lone pair then shares into the ring, giving a fourth, extra-stable form (every atom has an octet). Meta attack never gets this extra form.

**Why –NO2 sends the group meta:** ortho or para attack puts + on the carbon next to the already positive nitrogen of –NO2. Two + charges side by side is very unstable. Meta attack avoids this, so meta is the "least bad" route.

**Why halogens are the odd one out:** strong –I (pulls electrons) makes the ring slower, but their lone pairs (+R) still stabilise the ortho/para σ-complex. So: deactivating but ortho/para-directing.

**Methyl group:** +I effect and **hyperconjugation** (C–H σ electrons share into the ring) push electrons in. Toluene nitrates about 25 times faster than benzene and gives o- + p-nitrotoluene.

**Ortho vs para ratio:** para is usually the major product with a bulky group or bulky electrophile (steric hindrance at ortho).

```text
ORIENTATION FLOWCHART

 Does the atom joined to the ring have a lone pair, or is it an alkyl?
   ├─ YES → ortho/para director
   │        ├─ is it a halogen? → deactivating (–I wins on rate)
   │        └─ otherwise       → activating
   └─ NO, it is δ+ or carries + (C=O, N=O, C≡N, NR3+) → meta director, deactivating
```

*Pharmacy example:* making paracetamol, the –OH of phenol directs the nitro group para; reducing it gives p-aminophenol, which is acetylated to paracetamol.

## 1.6 Important derivatives: DDT, saccharin, BHC, chloramine

| Compound | Chemical name | Made from | Main use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DDT | p,p'-Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane | Chlorobenzene + chloral | Insecticide (malaria mosquitoes) |
| Saccharin | o-Sulfobenzimide (1,2-benzisothiazol-3-one 1,1-dioxide) | Toluene | Artificial sweetener |
| BHC | Benzene hexachloride = 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane | Benzene + Cl2 in UV light | Insecticide; γ-isomer lindane for scabies, lice |
| Chloramine-T | Sodium N-chloro-p-toluenesulfonamide | Toluene | Antiseptic, disinfectant, oxidising reagent |

**DDT**

```text
2 Cl–C6H5 (chlorobenzene) + Cl3C–CHO (chloral)  —(conc. H2SO4)→  (p-ClC6H4)2CH–CCl3 (DDT) + H2O

Structure: two p-chlorophenyl rings on one carbon, which also carries a –CCl3 group.
      Cl–C6H4
             \
              CH–CCl3
             /
      Cl–C6H4
```

The para positions are chosen because Cl is an o/p director and para has less crowding. DDT kills insects by keeping their nerve sodium channels open. It is now **banned or restricted** for farming because it does not break down, builds up in fat (bioaccumulation) and harms birds (thin eggshells). It is still allowed in limited indoor malaria spraying.

**Saccharin (Remsen–Fahlberg synthesis)**

```text
Toluene
  │  ClSO3H (chlorosulfonic acid)
  ▼
o-Toluenesulfonyl chloride  (+ para isomer, separated)
  │  NH3
  ▼
o-Toluenesulfonamide
  │  KMnO4 (oxidises –CH3 to –COOH)
  ▼
o-Sulfamoylbenzoic acid
  │  heat, –H2O (ring closes)
  ▼
Saccharin  (benzene ring fused to a 5-membered ring: C=O, N–H, SO2)
```

Saccharin is about **300–500 times sweeter than sugar** and gives no calories, so it suits diabetic and diet products. It is poorly soluble, so the **sodium salt** is used in tablets and syrups. It has a slight bitter aftertaste.

**BHC (benzene hexachloride, gammexane, lindane)**

```text
C6H6 + 3 Cl2  —(sunlight / UV, no catalyst)→  C6H6Cl6
```

This is a **free-radical addition**, not substitution; the ring loses aromaticity. Several stereoisomers form (α, β, γ, δ …). Only the **γ-isomer (lindane, \~12–15% of the mixture)** is strongly insecticidal. *Uses:* insecticide; 1% lindane lotion for **scabies and head lice**. Its use is now restricted because of nerve toxicity and environmental persistence. The name "benzene hexachloride" is misleading — it is a cyclohexane, not a benzene.

**Chloramine-T**

```text
Toluene —(ClSO3H)→ p-toluenesulfonyl chloride —(NH3)→ p-toluenesulfonamide
        —(NaOCl / NaOH)→  CH3–C6H4–SO2–N(Cl)− Na+   (chloramine-T)
```

In water it slowly releases **hypochlorite (active chlorine)**, which kills microbes. *Uses:* antiseptic for wounds and mouthwashes, disinfecting water, surfaces and instruments, and as an oxidising agent in drug analysis. It is gentler on tissue than bleach. (Dichloramine-T, the N,N-dichloro form, is a related antiseptic.)

```text
   ┌────────────────────────┬────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
 Structure                 Aromaticity            EAS                    Derivatives
 • Kekulé + flaws          • C-P-C-H              • 3-step mechanism     • DDT
 • resonance, 1.39 Å       • 4n+2 π e−            • nitration            • saccharin
 • sp2 orbital picture     • anti / non-aromatic  • sulfonation (rev.)   • BHC / lindane
 • 36 kcal/mol RE                                 • halogenation         • chloramine-T
                                                  • Friedel–Crafts
                                                  • substituent effects
```

# Unit 2: Phenols, aromatic amines and aromatic acids

One rule explains most of this unit: **anything that spreads out or pulls away a negative charge makes an acid stronger; anything that pulls away a lone pair makes a base weaker.** Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG, e.g. –NO2) therefore raise acidity and lower basicity; electron-donating groups (EDG, e.g. –CH3, –OCH3) do the opposite.

**Quick pKa scale (smaller pKa = stronger acid)**

| Compound | pKa | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) | 0.4 | As strong as a mineral acid |
| Benzoic acid | 4.2 | Carboxylic acid |
| Acetic acid | 4.76 | For comparison |
| Carbonic acid (H2CO3) | 6.4 | Decides NaHCO3 test |
| p-Nitrophenol | 7.2 | EWG raises acidity |
| Phenol | 10.0 | Weak acid |
| p-Cresol | 10.2 | EDG lowers acidity |
| Water | 15.7 |  |
| Ethanol | \~16 | Alcohols weaker than phenol |

## 2.1 Phenols

**Phenol** = C6H5OH, an –OH directly on a benzene ring (also called **carbolic acid**).

**Why phenol is acidic (more than alcohols):**

1. Phenol loses H+ to give the **phenoxide ion** C6H5O−.
2. The negative charge on oxygen spreads into the ring by resonance onto the **two ortho carbons and the para carbon**.
3. Spreading charge = a more stable ion = a stronger acid. In ethoxide (from ethanol) the charge stays stuck on oxygen.

```text
Phenoxide resonance (draw 4 forms + hybrid):

  O−            O              O              O
  |             ||             ||             ||
 benzene  <→  ring with −  <→  ring with − <→  ring with −
               at ortho C      at para C       at other ortho C
```

**Why phenol is weaker than carboxylic acids:** in carboxylate, the charge is shared by **two equal oxygens**. In phenoxide, three of the forms put the charge on carbon, which is less electronegative and holds it less happily.

**Practical test of acidity:** phenol dissolves in **NaOH** but does **not** react with **NaHCO3** (no fizzing), because phenol (pKa 10) is weaker than carbonic acid (6.4). Benzoic acid does fizz with NaHCO3. This separates the two in the lab.

**Effect of substituents on acidity of phenol**

| Substituent | Effect | Acidity vs phenol | Example (pKa) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| –NO2 at o/p | –I and –R; charge spreads onto NO2 oxygens | Much stronger | p-nitrophenol 7.2; picric acid 0.4 |
| –NO2 at meta | Only –I (no resonance to meta) | Stronger, less so | m-nitrophenol 8.4 |
| –Cl | –I | Slightly stronger | p-chlorophenol 9.4 |
| –CH3 | +I, hyperconjugation | Weaker | p-cresol 10.2 |
| –OCH3 at para | +R | Weaker | p-methoxyphenol 10.2 |

Order to memorise: **picric acid > 2,4-dinitrophenol > p-nitrophenol ≈ o-nitrophenol > m-nitrophenol > p-chlorophenol > phenol > p-cresol**. o-Nitrophenol is slightly weaker than para because its –OH is held by an **intramolecular hydrogen bond** to the nitro group, which makes the H harder to lose. The same H-bond makes o-nitrophenol **steam volatile**, which is how the o- and p-isomers are separated.

**Qualitative tests for phenol**

| Test | How to do it | Positive result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ferric chloride | Add neutral 1% FeCl3 to aqueous phenol | Violet colour (complex) |
| Bromine water | Add bromine water | White precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; colour of Br2 vanishes |
| Liebermann's nitroso test | Phenol + NaNO2 + conc. H2SO4, warm | Deep green/blue → red on dilution with water → blue again with NaOH |
| Phthalein test | Heat phenol + phthalic anhydride + conc. H2SO4; pour into NaOH | Pink-red (phenolphthalein forms) |
| Azo dye test | Add to cold benzenediazonium chloride in NaOH | Orange-red dye (p-hydroxyazobenzene) |

**Two named reactions often asked with phenol**

```text
Kolbe–Schmidt:  sodium phenoxide + CO2 (125 °C, 4–7 atm) → sodium salicylate —H+→ salicylic acid
                (salicylic acid → aspirin with acetic anhydride)

Reimer–Tiemann: phenol + CHCl3 + NaOH (60 °C) → salicylaldehyde (o-hydroxybenzaldehyde)
                (electrophile = dichlorocarbene :CCl2)
```

**Structure and uses of phenol and its relatives**

| Compound | Structure | Pharmaceutical uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phenol | C6H5OH | Antiseptic and disinfectant (Lister's carbolic acid); 0.5% preservative in injections; local anaesthetic in throat sprays; makes salicylic acid → aspirin; Bakelite |
| Cresols | Methylphenols (o-, m-, p-CH3C6H4OH) | Stronger disinfectants than phenol; Lysol (cresol + soap solution) for floors, instruments; m-cresol preservative in insulin |
| Resorcinol | 1,3-Dihydroxybenzene | Keratolytic (peels skin) in acne, eczema, dandruff lotions; antiseptic; makes fluorescein dye |
| α-Naphthol | 1-Hydroxynaphthalene | Molisch test for carbohydrates; azo dyes |
| β-Naphthol | 2-Hydroxynaphthalene | Azo dyes (coupling); antiseptic; once used against intestinal worms |

## 2.2 Aromatic amines

**Aniline** = C6H5NH2. Like ammonia, it is a base because the nitrogen has a **lone pair** that can grab H+.

**Why aniline is a weaker base than ammonia and aliphatic amines:**

1. The N lone pair is **delocalised into the ring** by resonance (shared with ortho and para carbons), so it is less available for H+.
2. The anilinium ion (C6H5NH3+) has no such resonance, so protonation loses this stabilisation.
3. The ring carbon is sp2 and pulls electrons (–I).

| Base | pKb (smaller = stronger) |
| --- | --- |
| Methylamine | 3.4 |
| Ammonia | 4.75 |
| Aniline | 9.4 |
| Diphenylamine | 13.1 |
| Triphenylamine | \~neutral |

Order: **aliphatic amines > NH3 > aniline > diphenylamine > triphenylamine**.

**Effect of substituents on basicity of aniline**

| Substituent | Effect | Basicity | Example (pKb) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| –CH3 (para) | +I, hyperconjugation pushes electrons to N | Stronger | p-toluidine 8.9 |
| –OCH3 (para) | +R | Stronger | p-anisidine 8.7 |
| –Cl (para) | –I | Weaker | p-chloroaniline 10.0 |
| –NO2 (meta) | –I | Weaker | m-nitroaniline 11.5 |
| –NO2 (para) | –I and –R (lone pair pulled to NO2) | Much weaker | p-nitroaniline 13.0 |

**Ortho effect:** nearly every ortho-substituted aniline (even o-toluidine) is a **weaker** base than aniline. The ortho group crowds the –NH3+ formed on protonation (steric inhibition of protonation and solvation).

## 2.3 Diazonium salts

**Diazotisation** — a primary aromatic amine reacts with nitrous acid at **0–5 °C**:

```text
C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2 HCl  —(0–5 °C)→  C6H5N2+ Cl− (benzenediazonium chloride) + NaCl + 2 H2O

Mechanism outline: NaNO2 + HCl → HNO2 → NO+ (nitrosonium)
                   ArNH2 + NO+ → Ar–NH–N=O (N-nitrosamine) → tautomerise → Ar–N=N–OH
                   → protonate, lose H2O → Ar–N≡N+
```

**Why ice-cold and why aromatic only:** aryl diazonium ions are stabilised by resonance with the ring, but above about 5 °C they lose N2 to form phenol. Aliphatic diazonium ions have no ring to share charge and decompose instantly. Diazonium salts are **used in solution immediately**; dry salts can explode.

**Synthetic applications — the "diazonium wheel"**

```text
                          C6H5N2+ Cl−
   ┌──────────────────┬────────────────┼─────────────────┬────────────────┐
 CuCl/HCl         CuBr/HBr         CuCN/KCN          KI                HBF4, heat
 C6H5Cl           C6H5Br           C6H5CN            C6H5I             C6H5F
 (Sandmeyer)      (Sandmeyer)      (Sandmeyer)                         (Balz–Schiemann)

   ┌──────────────────┬────────────────┼─────────────────┬────────────────┐
 H2O, warm        H3PO2 or EtOH    Cu powder + HCl   phenol, NaOH      aniline, mild acid
 C6H5OH           C6H6             C6H5Cl            p-hydroxyazo-     p-aminoazobenzene
 (phenol)         (deamination)    (Gattermann)      benzene (orange)  (yellow)
                                                     └── coupling reactions (N2 kept) ──┘
```

- **Replacement reactions** — N2 leaves, another group takes its place (Sandmeyer, Gattermann, KI, Balz–Schiemann, hydrolysis, reduction to benzene).
- **Coupling reactions** — N2 stays; the diazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile and attacks the para position of an activated ring (phenol in alkali, pH 9–10; amine in mild acid, pH 4–5). The product has an –N=N– (azo) group and is coloured.
- **Reduction with SnCl2/HCl** gives phenylhydrazine (C6H5NHNH2), used to identify sugars (osazones).

*Pharmacy links:* **Prontosil**, the first sulfa drug, is an azo dye; **methyl orange** indicator is made by coupling; the **Bratton–Marshall** assay of sulfonamides uses diazotisation + coupling to give a coloured product read in a colorimeter.

## 2.4 Aromatic acids (benzoic acid)

**Benzoic acid** = C6H5COOH, white crystals, found in gum benzoin.

**Acidity:** pKa 4.2. It is stronger than phenol because the benzoate ion shares its negative charge **equally between two oxygens** (two identical resonance forms). It is slightly stronger than acetic acid (4.76) because the sp2 phenyl group pulls electrons (–I), while the methyl of acetic acid pushes electrons in.

```text
Benzoate resonance:
   C6H5–C(=O)–O−   <→   C6H5–C(–O−)=O        (charge shared by two equal O atoms)
```

**Effect of substituents on acidity of benzoic acid**

| Substituent | Position | pKa | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| –NO2 | ortho | 2.2 | Ortho effect + –I |
| –OH (salicylic acid) | ortho | 3.0 | Intramolecular H-bond stabilises the anion |
| –NO2 | para | 3.4 | –I, –R stabilise anion |
| –NO2 | meta | 3.5 | –I |
| –Cl | para | 4.0 | –I |
| None (benzoic acid) | — | 4.2 | Reference |
| –CH3 | para | 4.4 | +I destabilises anion |
| –OCH3 | para | 4.5 | +R destabilises anion |

**Ortho effect:** almost any group at the ortho position makes benzoic acid **stronger**, whether it donates or withdraws. The ortho group pushes –COOH out of the ring's plane, so the ring can no longer donate electrons to it (steric inhibition of resonance).

**Typical reactions of benzoic acid**

| Reaction | Reagent | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Salt formation | NaOH or NaHCO3 (fizzes, CO2) | Sodium benzoate |
| Esterification | Ethanol + conc. H2SO4 | Ethyl benzoate (fruity smell) |
| Acid chloride | SOCl2 or PCl5 | Benzoyl chloride |
| Amide | Benzoyl chloride + NH3 | Benzamide |
| Reduction | LiAlH4 | Benzyl alcohol |
| Decarboxylation | Heat with soda lime (NaOH + CaO) | Benzene |
| Ring nitration | conc. HNO3 + H2SO4 | m-Nitrobenzoic acid (–COOH is a meta director) |

**Test:** neutral FeCl3 gives a **buff (pale brown) precipitate** of ferric benzoate. Salicylic acid gives violet instead (it also has a phenol –OH).

**Uses:** benzoic acid and **sodium benzoate** are preservatives in syrups and foods (work best below pH 4.5); **Whitfield's ointment** (benzoic acid 6% + salicylic acid 3%) treats ringworm; benzoyl peroxide treats acne; salicylic acid makes aspirin and methyl salicylate.

## 2.5 Unit 2 mind map

```text
                    PHENOLS · AMINES · ACIDS
   ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
 PHENOLS (acid, pKa 10)     AMINES (base, pKb 9.4)       BENZOIC ACID (pKa 4.2)
 • phenoxide resonance      • lone pair in ring          • 2 equal O resonance
 • EWG ↑ acidity            • EDG ↑ basicity             • EWG ↑ acidity
 • FeCl3 violet, Br2 ppt    • ortho effect ↓ basicity    • ortho effect ↑ acidity
 • cresol, resorcinol,      • diazotisation 0–5 °C      • reactions, FeCl3 buff
   naphthols                • Sandmeyer, coupling        • preservative
```

# Unit 3: Fats and oils

Fats and oils are **triglycerides**: one glycerol molecule joined by ester bonds to three fatty acids. Fats (ghee, lard, cocoa butter) are solid at room temperature because their fatty acids are mostly saturated; oils (groundnut, olive, castor) are liquid because their fatty acids are mostly unsaturated.

```text
Triglyceride (draw this):

   CH2–O–CO–R1
   |
   CH –O–CO–R2        R1, R2, R3 = long hydrocarbon chains of fatty acids
   |                   (same = simple glyceride; different = mixed glyceride)
   CH2–O–CO–R3
```

*Pharmacy examples:* castor oil (laxative), arachis/sesame oil (vehicle for oily injections), cod-liver oil (vitamins A and D), theobroma oil / cocoa butter (suppository base), wool fat (ointment base).

## 3.1 Fatty acids

Long-chain carboxylic acids, usually with an **even number of carbons** (made from 2-carbon units in nature) and an unbranched chain.

| Type | Name | Formula | Carbons : double bonds | Found in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Saturated | Butyric | C3H7COOH | C4:0 | Butter (gives its smell) |
| Saturated | Lauric | C11H23COOH | C12:0 | Coconut oil |
| Saturated | Palmitic | C15H31COOH | C16:0 | Palm oil, most fats |
| Saturated | Stearic | C17H35COOH | C18:0 | Animal fats, cocoa butter |
| Unsaturated | Oleic | C17H33COOH | C18:1 (Δ9) | Olive oil |
| Unsaturated (essential) | Linoleic | C17H31COOH | C18:2 (Δ9,12) | Sunflower, cottonseed |
| Unsaturated (essential) | Linolenic | C17H29COOH | C18:3 (Δ9,12,15) | Linseed oil |
| Unsaturated | Arachidonic | C19H31COOH | C20:4 | Animal tissue (prostaglandin source) |
| Hydroxy | Ricinoleic | 12-Hydroxyoleic acid | C18:1 + OH | Castor oil (\~90%) |

**Why unsaturated = liquid:** natural double bonds are **cis**, which put a kink in the chain. Kinked chains cannot pack tightly, so the melting point drops.

**Essential fatty acids** (linoleic, linolenic) cannot be made by the body and must come from food.

**Reactions of fatty acids:** (1) form salts (soaps) with alkali; (2) form esters with alcohols; (3) add H2 at double bonds (hydrogenation); (4) add halogens (I2, Br2) at double bonds — the basis of iodine value; (5) are oxidised at double bonds (rancidity).

## 3.2 Hydrolysis

Water splits the three ester bonds, giving glycerol and three fatty acids. It needs a catalyst: acid, superheated steam, or the enzyme **lipase** (as in digestion).

```text
Triglyceride + 3 H2O  —(H+ or lipase)→  Glycerol + 3 R–COOH (fatty acids)
```

## 3.3 Saponification

Hydrolysis with an **alkali** (NaOH or KOH). The fatty acids end up as their salts, which are **soaps**. It is irreversible.

```text
 CH2–OCOR                         CH2–OH
 |                                |
 CH –OCOR   + 3 NaOH  —heat→      CH –OH    + 3 R–COO− Na+
 |                                |              (soap)
 CH2–OCOR                         CH2–OH
                                (glycerol)
```

Sodium soaps are hard (bar soap); potassium soaps are soft (liquid soap, used in soft-soap and some liniments). Glycerol is the valuable by-product (humectant, solvent in syrups).

## 3.4 Hydrogenation (hardening of oils)

Hydrogen is added across C=C double bonds of an oil with **finely divided nickel** at about 150–200 °C and a few atmospheres.

```text
Oil (–CH=CH–)  + H2  —(Ni, 180 °C)→  Fat (–CH2–CH2–)
Example: triolein (liquid) + 3 H2 → tristearin (solid)
```

**Results:** liquid oil becomes semi-solid fat (vanaspati, margarine), melting point rises, iodine value falls, and the product resists rancidity. **Caution:** partial hydrogenation forms **trans fats**, which raise LDL cholesterol and heart-disease risk.

## 3.5 Rancidity

Rancidity is the **unpleasant smell and taste** a fat develops on storage.

| Type | Cause | What forms | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrolytic | Moisture + lipase enzymes (from microbes) | Free short-chain fatty acids | Butyric acid in stale butter |
| Oxidative (most common) | Air (O2) attacks double bonds; light, heat and metals (Cu, Fe) speed it | Peroxides → aldehydes and ketones (bad smell) | Old cooking oil, fish oils |
| Ketonic | Moulds act on saturated fats | Methyl ketones | Coconut oil, palm kernel oil |

**Mechanism of oxidative rancidity (free-radical chain, "autoxidation"):**

1. **Initiation** — light or a metal removes an H next to the double bond → lipid radical R•.
2. **Propagation** — R• + O2 → ROO• (peroxy radical); ROO• takes H from another lipid → ROOH (hydroperoxide) + new R•.
3. **Breakdown** — hydroperoxides split into smelly aldehydes and ketones.
4. **Termination** — two radicals combine; antioxidants stop the chain by donating H.

**Prevention:** store cool, dark and airtight (amber bottles, full containers, nitrogen flushing); keep dry; avoid copper/iron vessels; add **antioxidants** — BHA, BHT, propyl gallate, tocopherol (vitamin E), ascorbyl palmitate. *Pharmacy link:* this is why oily injections and vitamin capsules contain antioxidants and carry an expiry date.

## 3.6 Analytical constants

These numbers identify an oil, check its purity and catch adulteration. Each has a definition, a principle, a method and a meaning — learn all four.

**Formula symbols:** B = mL of titrant in the blank, S = mL in the sample, N = normality of titrant, W = weight of sample (g), 56.1 = molecular weight of KOH, 12.69 = 126.9 (equivalent weight of iodine) × 100 g basis / 1000 mL.

**(a) Acid value (AV)**

- **Definition:** mg of KOH needed to neutralise the **free fatty acids** in 1 g of fat or oil.
- **Method:** dissolve the weighed sample in neutralised ethanol–ether, add phenolphthalein, titrate with 0.1 N KOH to a pink end point.
- **Formula:** AV = (S × N × 56.1) / W
- **Meaning:** fresh oils have low AV; a high AV shows hydrolysis or rancidity. % free fatty acid (as oleic) ≈ AV / 2.

**(b) Saponification value (SV)**

- **Definition:** mg of KOH needed to **completely saponify** 1 g of fat or oil (free acids + esters).
- **Method:** reflux the sample with an excess of 0.5 N alcoholic KOH for 30–60 min. Back-titrate the leftover KOH with 0.5 N HCl (phenolphthalein). Run a blank without sample.
- **Formula:** SV = (B − S) × N × 56.1 / W
- **Meaning:** SV is **inversely proportional to the average chain length** (molecular weight). Short chains → high SV (coconut \~255, butter \~225); long chains → low SV (castor \~180). Mean molecular weight of the fat ≈ 168,300 / SV.

**(c) Ester value (EV)**

- **Definition:** mg of KOH needed to saponify the **esters** in 1 g of fat.
- **Formula:** EV = SV − AV. It tells how much true glyceride is present.

**(d) Iodine value (IV)**

- **Definition:** grams of **iodine absorbed by 100 g** of fat or oil.
- **Principle:** halogen adds across each C=C bond, so IV measures **unsaturation**.
- **Method (Wijs):** dissolve the sample in chloroform or CCl4; add Wijs reagent (iodine monochloride, ICl, in glacial acetic acid); keep 30 min in the dark. Add KI — unused ICl liberates I2. Titrate the I2 with 0.1 N sodium thiosulfate, starch indicator (blue → colourless). Run a blank. (Hanus method uses IBr.)
- **Formula:** IV = (B − S) × N × 12.69 / W
- **Meaning:** classifies oils — **non-drying** (IV < 100: olive, castor), **semi-drying** (100–130: cottonseed, sesame), **drying** (> 130: linseed). Drying oils harden in air and are used in paints and varnishes.

**(e) Acetyl value**

- **Definition:** mg of KOH needed to neutralise the acetic acid set free by hydrolysis of 1 g of **acetylated** fat.
- **Principle:** acetic anhydride acetylates free –OH groups, so the value measures **hydroxy fatty acids** (and free glycerol / partial glycerides).
- **Method:** boil the fat with acetic anhydride; wash out excess; find the saponification value of the acetylated fat.
- **Formula:** Acetyl value = (b − a) × 1335 / (1335 − a), where a = SV before and b = SV after acetylation.
- **Meaning:** castor oil has a very high acetyl value (\~145–150) because of ricinoleic acid; it identifies castor oil and detects its adulteration.

**(f) Reichert–Meissl (RM) value**

- **Definition:** mL of **0.1 N NaOH (or KOH)** needed to neutralise the **steam-volatile, water-soluble fatty acids** distilled from **5 g** of fat under fixed conditions.
- **Method:** saponify 5 g fat (glycerol–NaOH), acidify with H2SO4, steam-distil a fixed 110 mL, filter (insoluble acids stay on paper), titrate 100 mL of filtrate with 0.1 N NaOH.
- **Meaning:** measures **butyric and caproic acids**, found mainly in milk fat. Butter/ghee RM 17–35; most other fats < 1. Used to detect **adulteration of ghee** with vanaspati or animal fat.
- **Related:** **Polenske value** = the volatile but **water-insoluble** acids (caprylic, capric) left on the filter paper; high for coconut oil.

**Typical values (good for MCQs)**

| Oil / fat | Saponification value | Iodine value | RM value | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Coconut oil | 250–264 | 7–11 | 6–8 | Short-chain, saturated |
| Butter / ghee | 220–233 | 26–38 | 17–35 | High RM |
| Olive oil | 187–196 | 79–88 | < 1 | Non-drying |
| Castor oil | 176–187 | 82–90 | < 1 | High acetyl value |
| Groundnut (arachis) oil | 188–196 | 85–99 | < 1 | Injection vehicle |
| Cottonseed oil | 190–198 | 100–115 | < 1 | Semi-drying |
| Linseed oil | 188–196 | 170–200 | < 1 | Drying |

```text
   ┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
 FATTY ACIDS           REACTIONS                       ANALYTICAL CONSTANTS
 • saturated/unsat.    • hydrolysis → glycerol + FA    • Acid value → free FA (freshness)
 • cis kink → liquid   • saponification → soap        • Saponification value → chain length
 • essential FA        • hydrogenation (Ni) → vanaspati • Ester value = SV − AV
                       • rancidity: hydrolytic,        • Iodine value → unsaturation
                         oxidative, ketonic            • Acetyl value → free –OH (castor)
                       • antioxidants prevent          • RM value → butyric acid (ghee)
```

# Unit 4: Polynuclear hydrocarbons

Polynuclear (polycyclic) aromatic hydrocarbons have two or more benzene rings. They come in two kinds: **fused** rings sharing a side (naphthalene, anthracene, phenanthrene) and **isolated** rings joined through a carbon (diphenylmethane, triphenylmethane). Their chief source is **coal tar**.

| Compound | Formula | Ring pattern | π electrons | Resonance energy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Benzene | C6H6 | 1 ring | 6 | 36 kcal/mol |
| Naphthalene | C10H8 | 2 fused | 10 | 61 kcal/mol |
| Anthracene | C14H10 | 3 fused in a line | 14 | 84 kcal/mol |
| Phenanthrene | C14H10 | 3 fused, angled (bent) | 14 | 92 kcal/mol |
| Diphenylmethane | C13H12 | 2 rings on a CH2 | 6 + 6 | — |
| Triphenylmethane | C19H16 | 3 rings on a CH | 6 + 6 + 6 | — |

Fused systems are aromatic but **less aromatic per ring** than benzene (61 / 2 rings = 30.5 per ring vs 36). So their middle rings react more easily, often by **addition**, especially at the 9,10-positions of anthracene and phenanthrene.

## 4.1 Naphthalene

**Structure and numbering**

```text
          8      1                Positions 1, 4, 5, 8 = α (next to the shared carbons)
       7 / \  /  \ 2              Positions 2, 3, 6, 7 = β
        |   ||    |               Shared carbons = 4a, 8a (no H)
       6 \ /  \  / 3              Draw as two hexagons sharing one side,
          5      4                with three Kekulé forms possible.
```

- C10H8, white crystals, smell of moth balls, sublimes. Planar; all 10 carbons sp2; 10 π electrons (4n + 2, n = 2) → aromatic.
- Three resonance structures. Bonds are **not all equal**: C1–C2 = 1.36 Å (more double-bond character), C2–C3 = 1.42 Å.

**Synthesis 1 — Haworth synthesis (most asked)**

```text
Benzene + succinic anhydride
   │  AlCl3  (Friedel–Crafts acylation)
   ▼
β-Benzoylpropionic acid   (C6H5–CO–CH2CH2–COOH)
   │  Zn-Hg / HCl  (Clemmensen: C=O → CH2)
   ▼
γ-Phenylbutyric acid      (C6H5–CH2CH2CH2–COOH)
   │  conc. H2SO4, heat  (ring closure = intramolecular acylation)
   ▼
α-Tetralone
   │  Zn-Hg / HCl  (Clemmensen)
   ▼
Tetralin (1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalene)
   │  Se or Pd, heat  (dehydrogenation, –2 H2)
   ▼
Naphthalene
```

**Synthesis 2** — Industrially obtained from the middle oil fraction of **coal tar** (80–230 °C), crystallised and sublimed.

**Reactions of naphthalene**

*Electrophilic substitution prefers the α (1-) position.* Attack at C1 gives a σ-complex with **two** resonance forms that keep the other benzene ring fully intact; attack at C2 gives only **one** such form. More stable intermediate → faster reaction.

| Reaction | Reagent and condition | Main product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nitration | conc. HNO3 + H2SO4, 50 °C | 1-Nitronaphthalene |
| Bromination | Br2 in CCl4 (no catalyst needed) | 1-Bromonaphthalene |
| Sulfonation (low temp) | conc. H2SO4, 80 °C | Naphthalene-1-sulfonic acid (kinetic product) |
| Sulfonation (high temp) | conc. H2SO4, 160 °C | Naphthalene-2-sulfonic acid (thermodynamic product) |
| Friedel–Crafts acylation | CH3COCl, AlCl3 in CS2 | 1-Acetylnaphthalene |
| Friedel–Crafts acylation | CH3COCl, AlCl3 in nitrobenzene | 2-Acetylnaphthalene (bulky solvent complex) |
| Oxidation (strong) | O2/air, V2O5, 450 °C | Phthalic anhydride |
| Oxidation (mild) | CrO3 in acetic acid | 1,4-Naphthoquinone |
| Reduction | Na + ethanol | 1,4-Dihydronaphthalene |
| Reduction | Na + isoamyl alcohol (boiling) | Tetralin |
| Reduction | H2 / Ni, high temp + pressure | Decalin (decahydronaphthalene) |

**Why sulfonation changes with temperature:** at 80 °C the faster α-attack wins. The 1-sulfonic acid is crowded by the H at C8 (a **peri interaction**). At 160 °C sulfonation becomes reversible, so the less crowded, more stable 2-isomer builds up.

**Uses and medicinal relevance:** moth balls and insect repellent; phthalic anhydride (for phenolphthalein, plasticisers); naphthols and dyes. Drugs built on naphthalene: **naproxen** (NSAID), **propranolol** (β-blocker), **naphazoline** (nasal decongestant), **tolnaftate** (antifungal), **menadione** (vitamin K3 = 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone, a clotting vitamin).

## 4.2 Anthracene

```text
          8     9     1
      7 /  \  /  \  /  \ 2        Three rings fused in a straight line.
       |    ||    ||    |         Positions 9 and 10 (middle ring) = "meso" positions,
      6 \  /  \  /  \  / 3        the most reactive sites.
          5    10     4
```

- C14H10, colourless crystals with violet fluorescence; 14 π electrons; 4 resonance structures.

**Synthesis — Haworth / phthalic anhydride route**

```text
Benzene + phthalic anhydride
   │  AlCl3  (Friedel–Crafts acylation)
   ▼
o-Benzoylbenzoic acid
   │  conc. H2SO4, heat  (ring closure, –H2O)
   ▼
9,10-Anthraquinone
   │  Zn dust, distillation  (reduction)
   ▼
Anthracene
```

Other routes: from the **anthracene oil** fraction of coal tar; **Elbs reaction** (heating an o-methyl diaryl ketone); Friedel–Crafts of benzene with tetrabromoethane.

**Reactions — almost all at C9 and C10**, because attacking there leaves **two intact benzene rings** (most stable intermediate).

| Reaction | Reagent | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oxidation | Na2Cr2O7 / H2SO4 (or CrO3) | 9,10-Anthraquinone |
| Reduction | Na + ethanol | 9,10-Dihydroanthracene |
| Bromination | Br2 in CCl4 | 9,10-Dibromo-9,10-dihydroanthracene (addition) → heat → 9-bromoanthracene |
| Nitration | HNO3 in acetic acid | 9-Nitroanthracene |
| Diels–Alder | Maleic anhydride, heat | Adduct across C9–C10 (anthracene acts as a diene) |

**Medicinal relevance:** **anthraquinone laxatives** — senna, cascara, aloe and rhubarb contain anthraquinone glycosides (sennosides, emodin); **dithranol** (anthralin) for psoriasis; **anthracycline** anticancer drugs (doxorubicin, daunorubicin); alizarin dyes.

## 4.3 Phenanthrene

```text
             9 ── 10
           /         \            Three rings fused at an angle (bent like a "kinked" anthracene).
     8 ─ ring A    ring C ─ 1     The 9,10 bond in the middle ring behaves almost like
           \         /            an isolated C=C double bond.
            ── ring B ──
```

- C14H10, isomer of anthracene; 14 π electrons; **five** resonance structures, so it is **more stable** than anthracene (92 vs 84 kcal/mol).

**Synthesis 1 — Haworth synthesis**

```text
Naphthalene + succinic anhydride
   │  AlCl3, in nitrobenzene  (acylation at C2)
   ▼
β-(2-Naphthoyl)propionic acid
   │  Zn-Hg / HCl  (Clemmensen)
   ▼
γ-(2-Naphthyl)butyric acid
   │  conc. H2SO4  (ring closure)
   ▼
Cyclic ketone (tetrahydrophenanthrenone)
   │  Zn-Hg / HCl, then Se / heat  (reduce, then dehydrogenate)
   ▼
Phenanthrene
```

**Synthesis 2 — Pschorr synthesis:** o-amino-α-phenylcinnamic acid is diazotised (NaNO2/HCl, 0–5 °C); copper powder closes the ring → phenanthrene-9-carboxylic acid → heat (decarboxylation) → phenanthrene.

**Reactions — at the 9,10 bond:**

| Reaction | Reagent | Product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oxidation | CrO3 / acetic acid | 9,10-Phenanthrenequinone |
| Further oxidation | H2O2 or KMnO4 | Diphenic acid (biphenyl-2,2'-dicarboxylic acid) |
| Reduction | H2 / Pd (or Na + alcohol) | 9,10-Dihydrophenanthrene |
| Bromination | Br2 in CCl4 | 9,10-Dibromo-9,10-dihydrophenanthrene (addition) → heat → 9-bromophenanthrene |
| Nitration | HNO3 | Mixture, mainly 9-nitrophenanthrene |

**Medicinal relevance (very important):** the **cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene** (steroid) nucleus — phenanthrene, fully hydrogenated, with a five-membered ring attached — is the skeleton of **cholesterol, bile acids, sex hormones (oestrogen, testosterone, progesterone), corticosteroids (cortisone) and cardiac glycosides (digoxin)**. **Morphine and codeine** also contain a partly reduced phenanthrene skeleton.

## 4.4 Diphenylmethane

**Structure:** (C6H5)2CH2 — two benzene rings on one CH2. The CH2 is **benzylic** (next to two rings), so its hydrogens are reactive.

**Synthesis**

```text
1. C6H6 + C6H5CH2Cl (benzyl chloride)  —(AlCl3)→  (C6H5)2CH2 + HCl      [Friedel–Crafts]
2. 2 C6H6 + CH2Cl2  —(AlCl3)→  (C6H5)2CH2 + 2 HCl
3. 2 C6H6 + HCHO  —(conc. H2SO4)→  (C6H5)2CH2 + H2O
4. Benzophenone (C6H5)2C=O  —(Zn-Hg/HCl, Clemmensen)→  (C6H5)2CH2
```

**Reactions**

- **Oxidation** (CrO3 or K2Cr2O7/H2SO4) → **benzophenone**.
- **Side-chain bromination** (Br2, light) → diphenylbromomethane (C6H5)2CHBr.
- **Weakly acidic CH2** — a strong base (NaNH2) removes H+ to give the diphenylmethyl carbanion, stabilised over both rings.
- **Ring substitution** — each CH2-linked ring is activated (like toluene); nitration gives mainly **4,4'-dinitrodiphenylmethane**.

**Uses:** fragrance (orange-geranium odour) in soaps; the **diphenylmethyl (benzhydryl) group** appears in antihistamines **diphenhydramine, cyclizine, cetirizine, meclizine**, and in benztropine (antiparkinsonian).

## 4.5 Triphenylmethane

**Structure:** (C6H5)3CH — three benzene rings on one carbon. The three rings sit like a propeller and stabilise any charge or radical on the central carbon (trityl).

**Synthesis**

```text
1. 3 C6H6 + CHCl3  —(AlCl3)→  (C6H5)3CH + 3 HCl        [Friedel–Crafts]
2. C6H5MgBr + (C6H5)2C=O → (C6H5)3C–OMgBr —H3O+→ (C6H5)3C–OH (triphenylcarbinol)
                       —(HI or Zn / acetic acid, reduce)→  (C6H5)3CH   [Grignard route]
3. 3 C6H6 + CCl4 —(AlCl3)→ (C6H5)3CCl (trityl chloride) —reduce→ (C6H5)3CH
```

**Reactions — all at the central C–H**

| Reaction | Reagent | Product | Why it happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Oxidation | CrO3 / acetic acid | Triphenylcarbinol (C6H5)3COH | Weak tertiary benzylic C–H |
| Acidity | NaNH2 or Na | Trityl anion (C6H5)3C− Na+, blood-red | Charge spread over 3 rings |
| Chlorination | Cl2 | Trityl chloride (C6H5)3CCl |  |
| Trityl cation | Triphenylcarbinol + conc. H2SO4 | (C6H5)3C+, yellow solution | Very stable carbocation |
| Gomberg free radical | Trityl chloride + Zn or Ag | (C6H5)3C•, first stable free radical (Gomberg, 1900) | Radical spread over 3 rings |

**Uses:** parent of the **triphenylmethane dyes** — **crystal violet / gentian violet** (antiseptic, antifungal, Gram stain), **malachite green**, **brilliant green** (antiseptic), **basic fuchsin** (rosaniline, for Schiff's reagent), and the indicator **phenolphthalein** (once a laxative). The trityl group is in **clotrimazole** (antifungal) and is used to protect –OH groups in synthesis.

*Safety link:* bigger fused hydrocarbons such as **benzo\[a\]pyrene** (in cigarette smoke, burnt food, vehicle exhaust) are **carcinogenic**; the body oxidises them to epoxides that bind DNA.

```text
   NAPHTHALENE           ANTHRACENE         PHENANTHRENE        DIPHENYL-       TRIPHENYL-
   • α > β for EAS       • 9,10 reactive    • 9,10 like C=C     METHANE         METHANE
   • Haworth (succinic)  • phthalic         • Haworth, Pschorr  • FC benzyl Cl  • FC CHCl3, Grignard
   • SO3H 80 vs 160 °C     anhydride route  • steroid nucleus,  • → benzophenone• trityl +, −, •
   • V2O5 → phthalic     • → anthraquinone    morphine         • antihistamines• gentian violet dyes
     anhydride           • senna laxatives
```
